content: Percodan is a highly effective analgesic medication designed to manage moderate to severe acute pain, typically for short-term use. It is a combination drug that contains aspirin, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID), and oxycodone, a potent opioid agonist. The medication was first introduced to the U.S. market in 1950 by DuPont Pharmaceuticals and was once one of the most commonly prescribed pain relievers. Each Percodan tablet contains 4.8355 mg of oxycodone hydrochloride (equivalent to 4.334 mg of oxycodone base) and 325 mg of aspirin. Additionally, the tablets include inactive ingredients such as FD&C Yellow No. 10, FD&C Yellow No. 6, microcrystalline cellulose, and starch. The oxycodone component, chemically known as 14-hydroxy-7,8-dihydrocodein-6-one, is a white, odorless crystalline powder synthesized from the opium alkaloid thebaine. Thebaine itself has no therapeutic value. Oxycodone is metabolized in the body to form oxymorphone, and unlike morphine, it exhibits good oral bioavailability, similar to codeine. Before the introduction of acetaminophen (paracetamol), Percodan was a mainstay in oral pain management, particularly for postoperative pain, due to the potency and long half-life of oxycodone. Historically, the formulation also included a small amount of caffeine. The standard dosing regimen for Percodan is one tablet every six hours as needed for pain, with a maximum daily limit of 12 tablets. Over time, the use of Percodan has declined significantly, largely replaced by alternative oxycodone-containing compounds such as Percocet, which combines oxycodone with acetaminophen instead of aspirin. This shift occurred because aspirin and other NSAIDs can prolong prothrombin time, thereby inhibiting blood clotting and increasing the risk of postoperative complications like excessive bleeding. Other medications, such as Norco and Vicodin, which contain hydrocodone and acetaminophen, have also gained popularity for postoperative pain management. Hydrocodone is nearly as potent as oxycodone but is less strictly regulated than Percodan. In the United States, Percodan is classified as a Schedule II controlled substance under the Uniform Controlled Substances Act of 1970, alongside drugs like cocaine, morphine, and raw opium. Schedule II drugs are subject to strict regulations, including a prohibition on telephone prescriptions (except in emergencies) and no allowance for refills. In contrast, hydrocodone-containing medications like Vicodin and Norco are classified as Schedule III substances, which are less tightly regulated. Percodan has become increasingly obsolete in the U.S., with prescription rates declining sharply since the 1960s due to the availability of alternative oxycodone formulations, such as Percocet, Tylox, OxyContin, and Roxicodone. Despite its reduced use, Percodan is still sold under the brand name Endodan. All oxycodone-containing products, including Percodan, Percocet, and OxyContin, carry a significant risk of addiction and dependence. Oxycodone can lead to drug dependence similar to that of morphine and is therefore prone to abuse. It is highly sought after by individuals with opioid addiction. However, many addicts prefer OxyContin over Percodan or Percocet because OxyContin contains only oxycodone without additional active ingredients like aspirin or acetaminophen. As of 2008, both Percodan and Percocet are manufactured by Endo Pharmaceuticals.
